stem: What is an autoencoder trained to do?
choices: Classify its input into one of a fixed set of labels
Reproduce its own input at the output, after forcing it through a narrow middle layer
Predict the next item in a sequence from the items before it
Separate real examples from fakes produced by a second network
explanation: An autoencoder maps x to a compressed code and back to an approximation of x. The target is the input itself, which is why it needs no labels — and why the narrow middle is the only thing that makes the task non-trivial.

stem: Without its bottleneck, an autoencoder would learn nothing useful. Why?
choices: Because the loss function would have nothing to compare the output against
Because the decoder would have no input to work from
Because with enough width it could simply copy the input straight through, so it would never be forced to find what the data has in common
Because the gradient could not flow backwards through a wide layer
explanation: The narrow middle is the whole design. Fewer numbers than the input means the network must throw something away, and to reconstruct well it has to throw away the accidents and keep the structure.

stem: One word: what is the compressed internal representation at an autoencoder's narrowest point called — the ____ space?
explanation: Latent. The latent space is the compressed code the encoder produces and the decoder reads; nearby points in it decode to similar outputs, which is what makes it a map of the data rather than a filing cabinet.

stem: What is a latent space?
choices: The compressed internal representation a network learns, in which each point stands for an input and nearby points stand for similar inputs
The unused capacity of a network — the neurons that never activate
The set of all images the network has been shown during training
The space of possible weight values the optimiser searches
explanation: The latent space is where the data lives once the accidental detail has been stripped out. Its dimensions are learned rather than chosen, and the fact that it is continuous is what lets you move through it and get sensible outputs.

stem: What is the essential difference between an autoencoder and a variational autoencoder?
choices: An AE has a decoder; a VAE has only an encoder
An AE is trained with labels; a VAE is trained without them
An AE encodes each input to one fixed point in the latent space; a VAE encodes it to a probability distribution over the latent space, which you can then sample from
An AE works on images; a VAE works on text
explanation: A point versus a distribution. Because the VAE's encoder outputs a distribution rather than a single code, the latent space is filled in continuously, so a point you draw at random still decodes to something realistic.

stem: Why is a variational autoencoder generative when a plain autoencoder is not?
choices: Because the VAE is trained on far more data, so it has seen enough examples to invent new ones

Because you can sample a new point from the VAE's simple latent distribution and decode it into a new, realistic example that was never in the training set; the plain AE only has codes for inputs it was given
Because the VAE has a second network that judges whether its output looks real
Because the VAE's decoder is larger than its encoder
explanation: Generation is sampling. The VAE trains its latent space to look like a simple distribution, so drawing z from that distribution and pushing it through the decoder yields a new example. A plain AE's latent space has holes, and a point in a hole decodes to nothing meaningful.

stem: After a VAE has been trained, how is a new image actually produced?
choices: An existing image is passed through the encoder and the output is returned unchanged
The decoder is run backwards from a chosen label
The training images are averaged and noise is added to the result
A point z is drawn at random from the simple latent distribution and pushed through the decoder
explanation: Sample, then decode. Nothing is encoded at generation time: the randomness supplies the variation and the learned decoder supplies the structure, which is exactly the course's 'learn z to x, then crank the PRNG'.

stem: A VAE's training objective has two competing parts. What are they, and why must they compete?
choices: A reconstruction term, keeping the output close to the input, and a regularisation term, keeping the latent distribution close to a simple prior; reconstruction alone would scatter the codes and leave the space full of holes
A classification term and a clustering term, so the latent space is organised by class
A generator term and a discriminator term, played against each other
A forward-noising term and a reverse-denoising term
explanation: Reconstruction pulls the codes apart so each input is recoverable; regularisation pushes them back together into one simple, gap-free distribution. Generation needs both — a space you can sample from and a decoder that makes something of what you sample.

stem: An autoencoder lab is described as 'our first generative AI'. What is the honest verdict on that claim?
choices: Yes without qualification — reconstructing an image is generating an image
No in any sense — an autoencoder is a classifier

Yes in that it is the first architecture in the course that produces an output resembling its training data and contains a decoder you could sample from, but a plain AE only reconstructs; it takes the VAE's probabilistic latent space to make it genuinely generative
Yes, because it is trained without labels, and all unsupervised learning is generative
explanation: The autoencoder is the hinge of the course: it is where a network stops mapping input to label and starts mapping a compressed representation back to data. The decoder is a generator in waiting; the VAE supplies the distribution that lets you actually crank it.

stem: Where do the VAE and the U-Net sit on the arc from predictive to generative architectures?
choices: Both are purely predictive, alongside the MLP and the CNN
Both are purely generative, alongside the Transformer and the diffusion model
They form the representation bridge — they learn compact, structured representations that capture the underlying factors of the data, which is what makes both prediction and generation possible
Neither is on the arc; they are training techniques rather than architectures
explanation: MLP and CNN predict; Transformer and diffusion generate; VAE and U-Net are the bridge in between. The bridge's question is 'what is the underlying structure?', against prediction's 'what is most likely?' and generation's 'what could be?'.

stem: What makes a U-Net a U-Net rather than an ordinary encoder-decoder?
choices: Its encoder and decoder are trained separately, one after the other
Its latent space is probabilistic rather than deterministic
It has two decoders, one for shape and one for colour
Skip connections carry fine spatial detail from each encoder stage across to the matching decoder stage, so detail lost in the downsampling is restored on the way back up
explanation: Compressing to a bottleneck destroys exactly the pixel-level precision a segmentation mask needs. The skip connections hand that detail straight across, which is where the U in the diagram comes from.

stem: One word: what kind of connection carries fine spatial detail across the bottleneck of a U-Net, giving the architecture its shape?
explanation: A skip connection. It passes each encoder stage's output directly to the matching decoder stage, so high-level context from the bottleneck and fine detail from the early layers are combined when the output is reconstructed.

stem: A hospital needs each pixel of a scan labelled as tumour or healthy tissue. Which architecture is designed for that, and why?
choices: A U-Net, because its skip connections preserve the fine spatial detail an output that must be pixel-accurate requires
An MLP, because every pixel can be an input and every pixel an output
A transformer, because attention lets every pixel see every other pixel
A plain autoencoder, because it reconstructs the image exactly
explanation: Image segmentation is the U-Net's signature task, and medical imaging is where it was introduced. The output has the shape of the input, which is why the decoder must be handed back the detail the encoder discarded.

stem: What is the general idea of an encoder-decoder architecture, beyond the autoencoder case?
choices: Two networks compete, one producing candidates and one judging them
One network compresses the input into a representation, and a second expands that representation into the target — which may be the same thing, or a translation of it, or a mask over it
One network is trained first and its weights are frozen while a second is trained on top
One network is run twice, once forwards and once in reverse
explanation: Compress, then expand. The target need not be the input: encoder-decoder is how a sentence becomes its translation, an image becomes its segmentation mask, and a noisy image becomes a clean one.

stem: The encoder-decoder idea appears on the course's milestone list twice over, in 1997 and again around 2014. What was it used for that made it famous?
choices: Chess, where the encoder read the board and the decoder chose the move
Expert systems, where the encoder turned symptoms into rules
Face recognition, where the encoder produced a fingerprint of each face
Machine translation, including Google Translate: the encoder compresses a sentence in one language and the decoder expands it into another
explanation: Translation is the natural encoder-decoder task, because the output is the same meaning in a different form. The course pairs the 1997 encoder-decoder with the arrival of 'deep learning' around 2014 and the rebuilt Google Translate.

stem: A factory trains an autoencoder on images of correctly made parts only, then watches its reconstruction error in production. What is it detecting, and how?
choices: Anomalies: the autoencoder reconstructs what it has learned well, so a defective part reconstructs badly and the error spikes
Overfitting: a rising reconstruction error means the model has memorised the training set
Class imbalance: the error reveals which class is under-represented
Drift in the camera calibration, which the latent space measures directly
explanation: Anomaly detection is the classic use of a reconstruction error. The latent space has room only for the regularities of normal parts, so anything outside that distribution comes back distorted — and the size of the distortion is the alarm.

stem: How do a VAE and a diffusion model differ in what they learn?
choices: The VAE learns from images, the diffusion model from text descriptions
The VAE learns both directions — an encoder into a simple distribution and a decoder back out. A diffusion model prescribes the forward noising process and learns only the reverse
The VAE learns the reverse process and the diffusion model learns the forward one
Neither learns anything about the data distribution; both memorise the training set
explanation: Both end up with a map from a simple distribution to the data, but they get there by different learning games. Nothing is learned about the diffusion model's forward corruption — it is designed — and that is what makes the reverse a clean supervised target.

stem: One word: the half of an autoencoder that turns a latent code back into data, and which becomes the generator once the latent space is one you can sample from.
explanation: The decoder. The encoder compresses data into the latent space and is discarded at generation time; the decoder expands a latent point into an output, so it is the decoder alone that does the generating.

stem: An autoencoder needs labelled training data, because it has to be told what the correct output is.
choices: True
False
explanation: False. The correct output is the input itself, so an autoencoder supplies its own target and needs no labels. That self-supervision is why it can be trained on any pile of unlabelled images.

stem: Both an autoencoder's bottleneck and a zip file reduce the size of the data. What is the difference in kind?
choices: The autoencoder is faster, because it runs on a GPU
There is no difference; an autoencoder is a compression algorithm

Zip compression is lossless and general — it can restore any file exactly. The autoencoder is lossy and specific: it learns what matters in one kind of data and discards the rest, so the code is a representation rather than a copy
Zip compression is learned from data; the autoencoder's is fixed in advance
explanation: The autoencoder's loss is the point, not a defect. Discarding what does not generalise is exactly how the bottleneck ends up holding the underlying factors of the data, which a general-purpose compressor never finds.

stem: In a two-dimensional latent space trained on handwritten digits, the points form separated clusters by digit. What does moving smoothly between two clusters produce?
choices: An error, because the point lies between two classes and belongs to neither
The average pixel brightness of the two digits
A sequence of decoded images that morph gradually from one digit into the other, because the space is continuous and every point in it decodes to something
The same digit repeated, since the decoder rounds to the nearest cluster
explanation: A well-trained latent space is continuous, not a lookup table. That is the reason a VAE can generate: every point decodes to a plausible example, including points no training image ever occupied.

stem: One word: what is the narrow middle layer of an autoencoder called, the one that forces the network to compress?
explanation: The bottleneck. It holds fewer numbers than the input, so the network cannot copy the input through and must instead keep whatever generalises — which is how a latent representation gets learned at all.

stem: What is a denoising autoencoder trained to do, and what does that buy?
choices: Reconstruct its own input exactly, with a tighter bottleneck than usual
Generate new examples by sampling the latent space
Remove noise from its own weights during training
Reconstruct a clean input from a deliberately corrupted copy of it, which forces the learned features to be robust rather than a memorised copy
explanation: Corrupt the input, ask for the clean version back. The network cannot simply pass the input through, so the representation it learns has to capture what the data really are — a different route to the same discipline the bottleneck imposes.

stem: One word: the kind of autoencoder trained to reconstruct a clean input from a deliberately corrupted one.
explanation: A denoising autoencoder. The idea reappears at the heart of diffusion models, which are trained to undo noise one step at a time.

stem: What is required of an autoencoder that is not required of a general encoder-decoder?
choices: That the output be the input — y = x — usually enforced with a dimensional bottleneck, whereas the general case has y different from x and needs no bottleneck at all
A probabilistic latent space
A convolutional encoder
That it be trained on labelled data
explanation: The autoencoder is the special case where the target is the input. Drop that and the same pattern — input, representation, output — covers translation, summarisation, segmentation and captioning, with no compression required.

stem: Sequence-to-sequence learning made the encoder-decoder famous. Why does the course insist that sequence data is historical rather than fundamental to the idea?
choices: Because sequence models were later proved incorrect
Because the pattern is input to representation to output, and that applies equally to images, audio, graphs and video — translation merely happened to be where it became visible
Because sequences are too slow to process
Because the encoder-decoder was invented for images first
explanation: Machine translation gave the architecture its fame in 2014, but auto-associative networks had it in the 1980s and U-Nets and diffusion models use it on images. It is a general architectural pattern that sequences happened to popularise.

stem: Attention is described as the end of the fixed bottleneck in encoder-decoder models. What changed?
choices: The bottleneck was made wider, so more information fitted through it
The encoder was removed entirely
The decoder began attending to a whole sequence of encoder representations, weighted per output element, instead of reading one fixed-length summary vector
The bottleneck was moved to the decoder side
explanation: Compressing a whole sentence into one vector loses detail, and the longer the sentence the worse it gets. Attention lets the decoder look back at every encoder state and decide which matter now, which is the direct ancestor of self-attention in the Transformer.

stem: Where does a diffusion model sit in the encoder-decoder family?
choices: Outside it — diffusion has neither an encoder nor a decoder
It is an encoder only, since it compresses images into noise
It is frequently formulated as an iterative encoder-decoder, often a U-Net, that takes noise in and produces data
It is a decoder only, and the encoder is replaced by a discriminator
explanation: The denoiser at each step is usually a U-Net, so the same compress-then-expand pattern runs inside every one of the many steps. That is why the course treats the encoder-decoder as a single idea spanning autoencoders, Transformers, U-Nets and diffusion alike.

stem: The encoder-decoder story starts in the 1980s with auto-associative networks. What were they trained to do?
choices: Reproduce their own inputs, with a bottleneck hidden layer that was then found to hold a learned representation
Classify images into a fixed set of categories
Translate between two languages
Predict the next item in a sequence
explanation: Train a network to output what it was given, squeeze the middle, and the middle layer becomes a compact code. Rumelhart and colleagues in 1986 and Bourlard and Kamp in 1988 established the pattern that Hinton and Salakhutdinov deepened in 2006.

stem: Which ordering of the encoder-decoder genealogy is correct?
choices: Sequence-to-sequence, auto-associative networks, deep autoencoders, attention, Transformer
Attention, auto-associative networks, sequence-to-sequence, deep autoencoders, Transformer
Deep autoencoders, auto-associative networks, Transformer, attention, sequence-to-sequence
Auto-associative networks in the 1980s, deep autoencoders in 2006, denoising and sparse variants, sequence-to-sequence in 2013-14, attention in 2014-15, the Transformer in 2017
explanation: One idea, refined step by step: reproduce the input, make it deep, make it robust, make the output different from the input, remove the fixed bottleneck, then drop the recurrence. U-Net and the generative models branch off from 2015.

stem: Houses scattered along a winding road can be located by how far along the road they sit, instead of by two map coordinates. What does that picture illustrate?
choices: Overfitting — the description is too closely tailored to these particular houses
A latent space: a lower-dimensional description that keeps the information that matters and throws away the empty space around it
Data augmentation — new houses can be invented along the road
One-hot encoding — each house gets its own slot
explanation: The data do not fill the space they are drawn in, so fewer numbers suffice to say where each point is. That is exactly what the bottleneck discovers: ten inputs can often be carried by two, and expanded back again.

stem: Generating a new image means picking a random point in the latent space. Why does that make a plain autoencoder's latent space a risky place to sample from?
choices: Because the latent space is too small to hold a new image
Because sampling requires labelled data, which the autoencoder does not have
Because the decoder can only reproduce images it has already seen

Because a small step from a real example may land inside the region of realistic data or outside it, and nothing in the training makes the space between examples meaningful — which is why the VAE forces the codes into a well-behaved distribution you can sample from
explanation: A plain autoencoder is only ever asked to reproduce points it was given, so the gaps between them can decode to nonsense. The VAE's regularisation term is there precisely to fill those gaps, which is what turns a reconstructor into a generator.

stem: An autoencoder is drawn as a bow-tie. Why is the VAE's latent space, pulled into a compact round cloud, 'harder to walk off' than a plain autoencoder's?
choices: Because the VAE's latent space has more dimensions
Because the VAE stores every training image in its latent space
Because the regularisation packs the codes into one continuous region around the origin with no empty gaps, so a random or nearby point still decodes to something realistic
Because the VAE has no bottleneck
explanation: The bow-tie's knot is the bottleneck: high-dimensional pixels squeezed into a few latent numbers (two are enough for the digit demo) and then expanded again. A plain autoencoder scatters its codes with meaningless gaps in between. The VAE's pull toward a standard normal distribution makes the space round and gap-free, so sampling it stays on the data.
